what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat a type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer. It works by targeting a protein called HER2 that helps cancer cells grow. It can be used before or after surgery, and also for breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. It helps slow or stop cancer from growing.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under the skin, usually in your thigh. A healthcare provider, such as a nurse or doctor, will give you this injection at a clinic or infusion center. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each injection takes about 5 to 8 minutes. You will be watched by your healthcare team for at least 30 minutes after your first injection and at least 15 minutes after later injections to make sure you do not have a reaction.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. The usual schedule is one injection given every 3 weeks (every 21 days). Your first dose is a 'loading dose' which is a higher starting amount. After that, you will receive a lower 'maintenance dose' at each visit. Always follow your doctor's instructions and never skip or change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled appointment or dose, call your doctor or healthcare team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Try to keep all your appointments. If you miss a dose and it has been less than 6 weeks since your last dose, you can receive the maintenance dose and continue on your regular every-3-week schedule. If more than 6 weeks have passed, your doctor may need to restart you on the higher loading dose. Do not try to catch up on your own.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled only by your healthcare provider or clinic. You do not need to store it at home. The clinic will keep it refrigerated at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should not be frozen or shaken. If you ever receive a take-home supply for any reason, keep it in the refrigerator, protect it from light, and ask your pharmacist or nurse for specific instructions.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting this treatment. Avoid getting pregnant while taking this medicine and for at least 7 months after your last dose, because it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 7 months after your last dose. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of infection if your blood counts are low. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines during treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: shortness of breath, chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeat, swelling of the ankles or legs, sudden weight gain (more than 5 pounds in a week), severe allergic reaction signs such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or fainting. Also call your doctor if you have fever, chills, or signs of infection; numbness or tingling in hands or feet; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; or any unusual symptoms that worry you. During the injection, tell the nurse immediately if you feel warmth, itching, flushing, or discomfort at the injection site.
when_it_works: This medicine does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before your doctor can tell if the treatment is working. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular tests and check-ups. Keep all your scheduled appointments even if you feel well. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Do not use if you are pregnant. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant during treatment. Females of childbearing age must use effective birth control. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Heart problems: This medicine can weaken the heart. Your doctor will check your heart function with tests called echocardiograms or MUGA scans before and during treatment. Tell your doctor if you have a history of heart disease. Children: This medicine has not been studied in children and is not approved for use in patients under 18 years old. Older adults: Older patients may be monitored more closely for side effects, especially heart-related ones.
